slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
Theory courses have built up knowledge of Loire Valley's four sub-regions and nearly 30 AOCs; now it's time to visualize these abstract concepts. This course uses Mapbox GL JS + GeoJSON technology to interactively present the complete geographic structure of the Loire Valley — you can see every AOC boundary, river direction, and soil zone distribution, and click to explore each appellation's details.

Course Learning Objectives

🗺️ Four Sub-Region Geographic Integration

Build spatial memory for Nantais → Anjou-Saumur → Touraine → Centre through interactive maps

🌊 River Systems and Microclimates

Observe how the main Loire River and tributaries — Maine, Layon, Vienne, Cher, Indre, Sèvre — shape AOC boundaries

📐 AOC Nesting Relationships

Understand the geographic layering of multi-tier AOCs: Anjou → Anjou Villages → Savennières → Coulée de Serrant

🪨 Soil Zone Visualization

Cross-reference the map to understand the geological boundary between Anjou Noir vs Anjou Blanc, Tuffeau vs Schist

slides.2.content:
This site's Loire interactive map is rendered using Mapbox GL JS, with data sourced from France's INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité) official GeoJSON, combined with hand-corrected Cru-level boundaries. The map supports multi-level display and interactive exploration.

🌊 Layer 1: Sub-Region

  • Pays Nantais (blue): Muscadet series, Gros Plant
  • Anjou-Saumur (purple): Anjou, Saumur, Layon, Bonnezeaux, Savennières, Saumur-Champigny
  • Touraine (brown): Vouvray, Montlouis, Chinon, Bourgueil, Saint-Nicolas-de-Bourgueil
  • Centre-Loire (green): Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé, Menetou-Salon, Quincy, Reuilly

🍇 Layer 2: AOC (Appellation)

Displays specific AOC boundaries; clicking any AOC pops up a detail card (area, varieties, soils, style, typical producers).

🏆 Layer 3: Cru (Single Vineyard / Sub-AOC)

Displays Cru-level boundaries: Coulée de Serrant, La Roche-aux-Moines, Bonnezeaux, Quarts de Chaume Grand Cru, Chaume Premier Cru, etc.

🪨 Layer 4: Soil Zone

  • Tuffeau tuffstone (white)
  • Brioverian schist (black)
  • Kimmeridgian marl (golden yellow)
  • Silex flint (dark red)
slides.2.quiz.question: Which technology does this site's Loire interactive map use for rendering?
slides.2.quiz.explanation: This site uses Mapbox GL JS (vector tile layers) combined with INAO official GeoJSON data to render all appellation maps. Mapbox GL JS offers 60fps interactivity, crisp vector zoom, and highly customizable styles — currently the mainstream choice for wine map visualization.
slides.7.title: Map Reading Skills — Three Key Observation Points
slides.7.highlights.0.title: Rivers as Boundaries
slides.7.highlights.0.content: The main Loire River and tributaries Layon/Cher/Vienne often serve as AOC boundaries
slides.7.highlights.1.title: South-Facing Slopes First
slides.7.highlights.1.content: The south-facing slopes of the Loire's north bank are where top-tier wines concentrate (Savennières, Vouvray, Sancerre)
slides.7.highlights.2.title: Nested Pyramid
slides.7.highlights.2.content: Large AOCs contain smaller AOCs, which contain Crus, which contain single vineyards
slides.7.content:
Learning to "read" a wine map is more important than memorizing AOC names. The following three observation techniques help you quickly understand the structural logic of any wine region.

🌊 Observation 1: How Rivers Divide AOCs

Loire Valley AOC boundaries frequently follow river courses:

  • Main Loire: Separates Anjou Noir (south bank) vs Anjou Blanc (north bank); Vouvray (north bank) vs Montlouis (south bank)
  • Layon River: The entire Layon sweet wine zone follows the river valley
  • Vienne River: Chinon is in the Vienne valley; Bourgueil is on the north bank of the main Loire
  • Cher River: The large Touraine AOC spans the Cher valley

🧭 Observation 2: Slope Aspect (Exposure) Determines Quality

In the northern hemisphere, the ideal vine aspect is south-facing (exposé sud) — maximum sunshine, highest photosynthesis efficiency, optimal grape ripeness. The top AOCs in the Loire Valley are mostly located on south-facing slopes of the Loire's north bank:

  • Savennières: Steep south-facing slope, north bank of Loire
  • Vouvray: South-facing slope, north bank of Loire (east of Tours)
  • Sancerre: South-facing slope, highland on the west side of Loire

This is why the "north bank" often produces top-tier wines — contrary to intuition ("south is warmer") — the key is "sun-facing side," not direction.

📍 Observation 3: Nested Pyramid Structure

The French AOC system is a pyramidal nested structure; on a map the same vineyard may belong to multiple AOCs simultaneously:

  • Anjou Blanc (regional) → ~1,000 ha
  • ↳ Savennières (village-level) → 145 ha
  • 　↳ Coulée de Serrant (monopole vineyard) → 7 ha

Producers choose which level to bottle under. The higher the tier, the stricter the rules, the lower the yield, the higher the price.
slides.7.quiz.question: Why do the north banks of the Loire River tend to produce top-tier wines — rather than the warmer south bank?
slides.7.quiz.options.0: The north bank has a hotter climate
slides.7.quiz.options.1: The Loire River flows past the north bank
slides.7.quiz.options.2: The north bank has steep south-facing slopes — the ideal sun-facing aspect in the northern hemisphere
slides.7.quiz.options.3: The north bank has better grape varieties
slides.7.quiz.explanation: In the northern hemisphere, the ideal vineyard aspect is south-facing (exposé sud), because the sun shines from the south at an angle, and south-facing slopes receive near-90° incidence, maximizing photosynthesis efficiency. The steep north-bank slopes of the Loire face south, which is why top AOCs such as Savennières, Vouvray, and Sancerre are concentrated on north-bank south-facing slopes. This is one of the core principles of wine geography — the counter-intuitive structure of "north bank = south-facing = premier terroir."
slides.8.title: Level 4-2 Knowledge Test
slides.8.questions.0.question: The Loire Valley's four major sub-regions from west to east are?
slides.8.questions.0.explanation: Starting from the Atlantic estuary at Nantes and travelling upstream along the Loire: Pays Nantais (oceanic) → Anjou-Saumur (transitional) → Touraine (continental transition) → Centre-Loire (semi-continental). This west-to-east sequence corresponds to a gradual transition from oceanic to continental climate, with grape varieties and wine styles changing accordingly.
slides.8.questions.1.question: What is the geographic relationship between Vouvray and Montlouis-sur-Loire?
slides.8.questions.1.options.0: Two Crus of the same vineyard
slides.8.questions.1.options.1: North bank of Loire (Vouvray) vs south bank (Montlouis) — a mirror pair
slides.8.questions.1.options.3: Montlouis is a sub-AOC of Vouvray
slides.8.questions.1.explanation: Vouvray (north bank) and Montlouis-sur-Loire (south bank) face each other across the Loire River, less than 5 km apart, sharing the same Tuffeau tuffstone soil and using 100% Chenin Blanc for dry, off-dry, sweet, and sparkling styles. Because Montlouis has a smaller production and lower profile, its price is typically 70–80% of Vouvray — an excellent value proposition.
slides.8.questions.2.question: What defines the boundary between Anjou Noir (Black Anjou) and Anjou Blanc (White Anjou)?
slides.8.questions.2.options.2: Divided by geological boundary (schist vs tuffeau)
slides.8.questions.2.explanation: Anjou Noir and Anjou Blanc are geological zone concepts; the dividing line is roughly near the town of Saumur: to the west is Precambrian Brioverian schist (blue-black in color, hence "Noir"), to the east is Cretaceous Tuffeau tuffstone (snow-white, hence "Blanc"). This geological line determines Chenin style, red variety choices (Cabernet Franc is more common on Anjou Blanc), and other terroir differences.
slides.8.questions.3.question: Which AOC is the only Grand Cru in the Loire Valley?
slides.8.questions.3.explanation: Quarts de Chaume was elevated from AOC to Grand Cru status in 2011 — the only AOC in the Loire Valley to achieve this designation. Coulée de Serrant, though of exceptional quality, is a "single-vineyard AOC" (similar to Château-Grillet) and does not carry the official Grand Cru designation. Bonnezeaux is a "Cru AOC" but has no Grand Cru label.
